entries.question: Why was Saul rejected as king?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 13:9-14 has Samuel telling Saul his dynasty is ended because Saul offered the burnt offering himself instead of waiting. 1 Samuel 15:11, 23 has Yahweh declaring he regrets making Saul king because Saul spared Agag and the best Amalekite livestock instead of completing the genocide. The two chapters give two different rejection events with two different stated causes.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook duplication problem in the books of Samuel. Saul gets rejected twice — once in 1 Samuel 13 for premature sacrifice at Gilgal, and once in 1 Samuel 15 for incomplete extermination of the Amalekites. Each rejection narrative is structurally complete: a divine command, a failure, a prophetic confrontation, and a declaration that Yahweh has rejected Saul as king. Critical scholarship — going back to Wellhausen and forward through McCarter, Klein, and Antony Campbell — has read these as parallel rejection traditions preserved side by side, not as a sequential narrative of progressive divine displeasure.

The apologist harmonization, found in Tsumura's NICOT and in most evangelical Samuel commentaries, treats the two rejections as sequential: in chapter 13 Saul's dynasty is rejected (his sons won't inherit the kingship), and in chapter 15 Saul himself is rejected (Yahweh tears the kingdom from him personally). That distinction works as a reading move, but it requires you to take very similar prophetic-rejection language in both chapters and assign it different referents based on what the later narrative requires. In 1 Samuel 13:14 Samuel says 'thy kingdom shall not continue' (lo' taqum mamlakhtekha) — a dynastic claim. In 1 Samuel 15:23 Samuel says 'he hath also rejected thee from being king' (vayyim'asakha mi-melekh) — a personal claim. The two rejections do differ on this point, and the apologetic reading captures that distinction.

But the larger problem is that both chapters are structured as the moment of decisive divine repudiation. The narrative in 1 Samuel 15:11 has Yahweh saying 'It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king' — and that's framed as the actual turning point, with no reference back to chapter 13 as an earlier rejection. Samuel and Saul never see each other again after chapter 15 (per 15:35), and David's anointing happens immediately in chapter 16 as the direct consequence of the chapter 15 rejection. The narrative treats chapter 15 as the cause of the dynastic change, not chapter 13.

McCarter's Anchor Bible 1 Samuel treats this as a duplication produced by the joining of independent source traditions about Saul's downfall. Antony Campbell's FOTL volume and Klein's WBC see the same pattern. There were probably multiple traditions in early Israel about why the house of Saul failed, and the redactor included both prominent ones — the sacrifice tradition and the Amalek tradition — without forcing them into a single chronology of sin. The harmonizer's 'dynasty rejected first, person rejected second' reading is grammatically possible, but it's a smoothing move imposed on what looks like a redactional doublet. The parsimonious reading is that the canon preserves two separate rejection traditions, and the question 'why was Saul rejected?' depends on which tradition you read.

entries.question: Was Haman an Agagite?
entries.summary: Esther 3:1 calls Haman "the Agagite," implying descent from Agag the Amalekite king. But 1 Samuel 15:7-8, 32-33 explicitly says Saul and Samuel wiped out every Amalekite man, woman, infant, and suckling, with Samuel personally hacking Agag to pieces. If the herem command was carried out as described, Agag's line cannot still be producing court villains in Persia roughly five centuries later.
entries.commentary:
Here's the setup the text is asking you to accept. 1 Samuel 15 has Yahweh ordering total annihilation of Amalek — herem, the ban, no survivors. Saul "utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword," Agag gets executed personally by Samuel, and Samuel's parting line to Agag is "as the sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women." That is a textually emphatic, no-loose-ends ending. Then five hundred years later in Esther 3:1, Haman shows up with the tag "the Agagite," and 1 Samuel 15:33's promise that Agag's line is over runs straight into a wall.

The apologist move here is to treat "Agagite" as either a tribal title for Amalekites broadly or a literary device. Gleason Archer in his Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties argues that some Amalekites obviously survived because they show up again in 1 Samuel 27, 1 Samuel 30, and 1 Chronicles 4:43 — so "Agagite" must just mean "of Amalekite stock." Carol Bechtel and Jon Levenson go a different route: Esther is consciously building a literary frame where Mordecai the Benjaminite (descendant of Kish/Saul) finally finishes the job Saul botched against Agag/Amalek. Mordecai is "son of Kish" in Esther 2:5, Haman is "the Agagite" in 3:1 — the author is signaling a Saul-vs-Agag rematch, not a genealogical claim.

The literary-frame reading is the most parsimonious one, and that is the consensus position in critical scholarship. But notice what it concedes. It concedes that the Chronicler and the Deuteronomistic Historian's own text — claiming a complete extermination — was not a factual report. The genealogy in Esther only makes sense as literary echo because the herem narrative is itself stylized, not historical. So the apologist who needs 1 Samuel 15 to be a faithful war report and Esther 3 to be straight history at the same time is the one stuck. Either the Amalekites weren't actually annihilated (in which case 1 Samuel 15's emphatic "utterly destroyed all" is wrong on its own terms), or Esther's "Agagite" is a literary tag rather than a lineage (in which case Esther is doing midrash on the Saul cycle and not reporting genealogy).

The surface contradiction resolves either way, but it resolves at the cost of one of the two texts being historically reliable. The text wants you not to notice that. Once you read 1 Samuel 15 as the Deuteronomist's polemic against Saul and Esther as a diaspora festival novella, the tension dissolves — but so does the historicist reading both texts depend on.

entries.question: How many sons did Jesse have?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 16:10-11 and 17:12 give Jesse eight sons — seven who pass before Samuel plus David the youngest. 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 names David as the seventh son, listing seven total. The two texts disagree by one son with no internal harmonization offered.
entries.commentary:
The numbers don't match and the disagreement is in the same canonical history. Samuel's anointing scene in 1 Samuel 16 has Jesse parade seven sons past Samuel, none get chosen, and then "there remaineth yet the youngest," David — eight total. 1 Samuel 17:12 backs this up: "he had eight sons." Then the Chronicler in 1 Chronicles 2:13-15 names them by birth order — Eliab, Abinadab, Shimea, Nethaneel, Raddai, Ozem — "David the seventh." Seven sons. One missing.

The traditional harmonization is that one son died young without offspring and so the Chronicler, who is doing genealogy not biography, omitted him. Keil and Delitzsch propose this, Gleason Archer repeats it, Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Exegetical Library Chronicles commentary defends it. The strongest version of that argument leans on the Chronicler's known habit of trimming genealogies for theological focus — he routinely compresses lists, skips generations, and ignores figures who don't serve his Davidic-cultic agenda. The targumic and rabbinic tradition went further and invented a son named Elihu to fill the slot (1 Chronicles 27:18 mentions an "Elihu, of the brethren of David" — possibly a seventh non-David brother, which would make eight, possibly a textual ghost).

Here's where the harmonization gets thin. The Chronicler is not just omitting a brother quietly — he is counting. He says "David the seventh." That is an ordinal claim, not a partial list. To make this work you have to assume the Chronicler knew of an eighth son, intentionally dropped him from the count, and then renumbered David from eighth to seventh in violation of his Samuel source. That is not omission; that is renumbering. Sara Japhet's commentary on Chronicles flags exactly this — the Chronicler routinely reshapes inherited material to fit a structural scheme, and the seven-son count is the structure, not an accident. Ralph Klein's Hermeneia volume on 1 Chronicles makes the same point: the discrepancy is best explained as the Chronicler conforming the Davidic family to a seven-son ideal, not a brother dying young.

The parsimonious read is that 1 Chronicles is a tendentious recasting of the Samuel tradition, and the numbers diverge because the Chronicler had a literary scheme to serve. The dead-brother hypothesis is post-hoc; the text gives you zero evidence of any such death, and the Chronicler himself never alludes to it. The apologetic answer requires inventing a corpse to save a count.

entries.question: Was David a man of war before he fought Goliath?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 16:18 introduces David to Saul as already "a mighty valiant man, and a man of war." One chapter later, 1 Samuel 17:33 has Saul calling David a youth incapable of fighting Goliath, and David unable to even walk in armor he has never tried on. The same David is veteran warrior and untested boy across consecutive chapters.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the classic seams in 1 Samuel where the doublet shows through. In chapter 16 David gets introduced to Saul by one of Saul's servants — "I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, that is cunning in playing, and a mighty valiant man, and a man of war, and prudent in matters." David is a known combat-experienced figure, joins Saul's court, becomes armor-bearer, plays the harp to chase off the evil spirit. Then chapter 17 opens and Saul doesn't recognize David, calls him a "youth," tells him he cannot possibly fight Goliath because he has no combat experience, and David himself confirms it by being unable to function in armor.

The apologist read is sequence-and-tone. Archer argues "man of war" was hyperbolic description by an admiring servant — David had killed a lion and a bear (1 Samuel 17:34-36) and that was good enough to call him a warrior, even though he had never faced an army. Walter Kaiser in Hard Sayings of the Bible takes the same line. The harder apologetic move is to compress the timeline: the encounter in chapter 16 was brief, Saul's mental state was deteriorating, he didn't really remember David, and so the "who is this youth" of 17:55 is just Saul fishing for genealogy, not personal identity.

None of that holds up against the actual textual evidence. The Septuagint (specifically Codex Vaticanus, LXX-B) is shorter than the Masoretic Text in this section — it omits 1 Samuel 17:12-31 and 17:55-18:5, exactly the passages that create the contradiction. P. Kyle McCarter Jr. in the Anchor Bible volume argues persuasively that LXX-B preserves an earlier shorter recension and the MT is a conflation of two originally independent David-introduction traditions — one where David joins court as a musician/armor-bearer, one where he arrives as an unknown shepherd to fight Goliath. The redactor stitched them together without smoothing out the inconsistency. Emanuel Tov in Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible takes the same position. Dominique Barthelemy's contribution to the OBO 73 Story of David and Goliath volume splits with McCarter and argues for MT priority, but acknowledges the doublet problem.

So the contradiction is real and it has a known mechanical cause: two source narratives, one redactor, no smoothing. The apologetic hyperbole defense doesn't engage the textual evidence at all — it just papers over the seam. When you have a manuscript witness that lacks the contradicting passages and a redaction-critical account of how the conflation happened, the burden is on the harmonizer to explain why the simpler textual solution should be rejected. Archer's response is essentially that LXX-B is corrupt, which is the opposite of what every major textual critic of Samuel concludes.

entries.question: How did David kill Goliath?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 17:49-50 says David killed Goliath with a sling and a stone and that "there was no sword in the hand of David." The very next verse, 1 Samuel 17:51, has David running over, drawing Goliath's own sword, and killing him with it. Within two verses Goliath dies twice by two different weapons.
entries.commentary:
Read the verses back to back and the tension is right there on the page. Verse 50 closes with an emphatic editorial summary: "David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and smote the Philistine, and slew him; but there was no sword in the hand of David." That's a definitive statement of cause of death. Then verse 51 immediately has David running up, taking Goliath's sword out of its sheath, "and slew him." The root in both verses is the same — mwt, "to die/kill" — though the stems differ (hiphil wayemitehu in v. 50, polel waymotetehu in v. 51), and both verbs translate as "and he killed him."

The standard harmonization treats verse 50 as a summary statement and verse 51 as the detail. Archer, Kaiser, and Tsumura in the NICOT volume all argue that the stone knocked Goliath unconscious or wounded him fatally, and the sword stroke was the coup de grace. Tsumura specifically argues that the Hebrew narrative regularly uses summary-then-detail structure and verse 51's "slew him" should be read as "finished him off." That is at least a coherent reading of the Hebrew syntax.

The problem with the harmonization is verse 50's explicit clause "there was no sword in the hand of David" — that is the narrator inserting a comment for emphasis, not a summary of stage-one of a two-stage kill. The narrator is signaling that the manner of death matters theologically: the LORD saves not by sword but by sling. Then verse 51 walks that back. McCarter notes again that the doublet problem is at work here too — verses 12-31, 50, and 55-18:5 are all in the MT "plus" material relative to LXX-B. The shorter Septuagint reading drops verse 50 entirely. If you take LXX-B as primary, the contradiction disappears because verse 50 was added later and clashed with the original verse 51.

So the apologist has to either accept that one of the two kill-statements is a redactional gloss (which makes the canonical text a stitched document), or insist that "there was no sword in the hand of David" was a stylistic flourish the narrator immediately undermined. Take your pick. The textual data strongly favors the redactional explanation. The harmonization is grammatically possible but it requires the narrator to mean the opposite of what he just emphatically said.

entries.question: Who killed Goliath?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 17 credits David with killing Goliath of Gath. 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim killed Goliath the Gittite, identifying Goliath specifically by the same weapon-description ("the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam") used for Goliath in 1 Samuel 17:7. The Chronicler in 1 Chronicles 20:5 "fixes" the problem by inserting "the brother of" before Goliath's name — a transparent harmonization.
entries.commentary:
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:19 is the smoking gun. It reads, without ambiguity, that Elhanan ben Jaare-oregim the Bethlehemite slew et-golyat hag-gitti — Goliath the Gittite — and the spear description matches 1 Samuel 17:7 word for word. The Chronicler, writing centuries later and aware that this clashes with the famous David-vs-Goliath story, rewrites the verse to read "Elhanan son of Jair slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite." Look at the Hebrew: the Chronicler took beit-ha-lakhmi ("the Bethlehemite") from 2 Samuel and reparsed it as et-lakhmi akhi ("Lahmi the brother of"). It's a literal letter-shuffle harmonization in the Chronicler's source text.

The apologetic response is the standard appeal to textual corruption: 2 Samuel 21:19 is scribally damaged and 1 Chronicles 20:5 preserves the original reading. Archer takes this line, so does the NIV Study Bible footnote, so does Tsumura in NICOT. The textual argument is that a scribe miscopied the original "Lahmi the brother of Goliath" as "Bethlehemite Goliath," creating a phantom contradiction.

The critical scholarship reverses the direction of dependence. McCarter, Anderson in the WBC volume on 2 Samuel, and Auld in the OTL volume on Samuel all argue 2 Samuel 21:19 is the older, harder reading and 1 Chronicles 20:5 is the smoothing. The principle is lectio difficilior potior — the more difficult reading is more likely original, because scribes harmonize toward coherence, not toward awkward contradictions. The Elhanan-killed-Goliath reading is theologically embarrassing; nobody would invent it. The Chronicler's fix is theologically convenient; that's exactly what a later editor would produce. Add to that the parallel verse in 2 Samuel 23:24 listing "Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem" as one of David's mighty men — possibly the same Elhanan, possibly a doublet — and the original tradition starts to look like Elhanan was the actual Goliath-killer and David inherited the feat in a later legendary expansion.

The parsimonious account is the one almost every critical scholar offers: Elhanan killed Goliath in the older tradition, the David-Goliath story is a secondary literary development (or transferred legend), and the Chronicler did exactly the kind of harmonization that betrays awareness of the underlying problem. The apologetic "scribal error" defense reverses the textual-critical principles it claims to apply, and it requires the Chronicler to have access to a manuscript reading nobody else had — except, conveniently, the one that resolves the embarrassment.

entries.question: When did Saul meet David?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 16:21-23 has David enter Saul's court as a beloved armor-bearer and harpist whom Saul personally requests from Jesse. One chapter later, 1 Samuel 17:55-58 has Saul not knowing who David is after the Goliath fight, asking Abner whose son this youth is, and then asking David himself. The same king either knows David well or has never seen him.
entries.commentary:
This is the same doublet problem as entry 223, viewed from Saul's angle. 1 Samuel 16:21-23 is unambiguous: David comes to Saul, stands before him, Saul loves him "greatly," makes him armor-bearer, sends a formal note to Jesse asking that David stay in court, and David is the personal music therapist who calms Saul's evil-spirit episodes. That is a deep working relationship. Then in 17:55 Saul watches David go out against Goliath and asks Abner, "whose son is this youth?" Abner — captain of Saul's entire army, who would have known the king's armor-bearer — also has no idea. After the fight, Saul asks David personally: "whose son art thou, thou young man?"

The apologetic harmonization runs in two flavors. Flavor one (Archer, Kaiser): Saul wasn't asking who David was, he was asking about David's family for the purpose of the reward in 17:25 (whoever kills Goliath gets the king's daughter and tax exemption for the father's house). Flavor two (Youngblood, Tsumura): Saul's mental deterioration was such that he genuinely didn't recognize his own armor-bearer, plus David had visibly aged or changed appearance during the gap.

Flavor one fights the text. Saul's question to Abner — "whose son is this youth?" — uses ben-mi zeh ha-na'ar, the phrasing for personal identification, and Abner's answer is "as thy soul liveth, O king, I cannot tell." That is not bureaucratic genealogy-gathering; that is Abner saying he doesn't know who the kid is. If David were Saul's armor-bearer, Abner's response is impossible. Flavor two requires Saul's mental deterioration to extend to Abner as well, and to all of Saul's court, which is a stretch.

The critical-scholarship answer is the same as the Goliath-doublet case. McCarter, Auld, and Hertzberg all argue 1 Samuel 16:14-23 and 1 Samuel 17 reflect two originally independent David-court-entry traditions that the redactor placed side by side. LXX-B omits the verses that create the worst contradictions (17:55-18:5). The MT preserves the conflation; LXX-B preserves an earlier shorter tradition. That is not an apologetic-friendly explanation, but it is the one that fits the manuscript evidence and the seam analysis. Saying Saul had two completely different first encounters with David is exactly what you would expect if the text is two stitched traditions, and it is exactly what you would not expect if a single coherent history was being told.

entries.question: How many Philistine foreskins did David buy his first wife with?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 18:27 says David killed 200 Philistines and brought back their foreskins to Saul as the bride-price for Michal. 2 Samuel 3:14 quotes David himself claiming he paid 100 foreskins. The text disagrees with itself, and David's own retrospective is half the original number.
entries.commentary:
Saul originally asked for 100 (1 Samuel 18:25). David delivered 200. Years later, asking for Michal to be returned to him after Saul's death, David says in 2 Samuel 3:14, "deliver me my wife Michal, which I espoused to me for an hundred foreskins of the Philistines." He cites the original demand, not the actual delivery.

The apologetic move here is straightforward and not crazy: David is referencing the contractual price Saul set, not the bonus he threw in. Archer and Youngblood both run this line. McCarter actually concedes it has some force — David's framing in 2 Samuel 3 is legal-formal, referring to the bride-price as covenanted rather than as delivered.

But there is a textual wrinkle that complicates the harmonization. The Septuagint and 4QSam-a both read 100 in 1 Samuel 18:27 as well, not 200. So one branch of the Hebrew tradition has David delivering exactly what was asked, and the contradiction simply doesn't exist there. The MT preserves the inflated 200 — possibly an early scribal enhancement of David's prowess, possibly the original. McCarter argues 100 is original and 200 is a glorifying expansion. Auld and Anderson lean the same way.

This one is a soft contradiction. If you accept MT as primary, you get a real number-clash that requires the "legal price vs. delivered amount" harmonization to resolve. If you accept the Qumran/LXX reading at 100, the numbers match and there is no contradiction. Either way you concede something — either the text has internal inconsistency or the text has manuscript variation. The apologetic move that wants both MT inerrancy and harmonized numbers needs to do work on both fronts. That is of course a textual-critical judgment call, but the manuscript evidence is what it is.

entries.question: When did Saul become David's enemy?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 18:8-9 says Saul began to eye David with suspicion immediately after the women's song crediting David with greater slaughter than Saul — "Saul has slain his thousands and David his ten thousands." 1 Samuel 18:27-29 marks the turn after the foreskin bride-price, when "Saul became David's enemy continually." The text gives two different ignition points for the rivalry within the same chapter.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 18 is a notorious chapter for narrative ordering. The women's song happens in verse 8, Saul "eyed David from that day and forward" in verse 9, and Saul's first attempt to kill David with a spear comes in verse 11. Then verses 12-16 narrate ongoing fear of David, the Merab-then-Michal marriage plot to use Philistines to kill David is verses 17-25, the foreskins are delivered in verse 27, and the chapter's summary in verse 29 says Saul "became David's enemy continually."

The apologist read here is the easiest of the bunch — the chapter is describing escalation. Saul's initial suspicion in verse 8 evolves into ongoing fear in verses 12-16 and finally hardens into continual enmity in verse 29. Tsumura and Youngblood both argue the contradiction is the SAB reading too much into a literary-summary phrase. There's some force to that. The word "continually" in verse 29 reasonably reads as the endpoint of the escalation, not a fresh beginning.

Where it gets interesting is the manuscript evidence again. LXX-B is significantly shorter through 1 Samuel 18 than the MT, omitting verses 10-11 (the first spear-throw), verses 17-19 (the Merab episode), and parts of verses 21, 26-27, and 29-30. The shorter LXX preserves a cleaner narrative: song-in-18:7, Saul's suspicion, Michal plot, foreskins delivered, full enmity. McCarter argues again that LXX-B is more original and MT is conflation. If you read the MT as primary you get a chapter that escalates messily across multiple ignition points; if you read LXX-B as primary the escalation is single-tracked.

This one is a soft contradiction. If the contradiction is just "the chapter has two summary statements about when the enmity started," the apologetic escalation read works fine. If the contradiction is "the chapter is internally chaotic because it conflates source material," the critical-scholarship account is more parsimonious. I lean toward calling this a poorly-formed contradiction question — the chapter is messy, but "messy" is not the same as "contradictory." That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. The SAB framing overstates a real seam problem as a binary contradiction.

entries.question: When did "Is Saul among the prophets?" become a proverb?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 10:11-12 gives the origin of the proverb "Is Saul also among the prophets?" when Saul prophesies among Samuel's prophet band shortly after his anointing. 1 Samuel 19:24 gives a second, independent origin story for the same proverb — Saul stripping naked and prophesying before Samuel while pursuing David. Two different etiologies for the same saying.
entries.commentary:
These are classic etiological doublets. Both passages explicitly say "wherefore they say" or "it became a proverb" — the narrator is anchoring a folk-saying to a specific event. The problem is they anchor it to two different events. In 1 Samuel 10, Saul is freshly anointed, has a positive spirit-experience among the prophets at Gibeah, and the saying captures public surprise that the new king has a prophetic streak. In 1 Samuel 19, Saul has gone full antagonist, his messengers all get caught in prophetic ecstasy when sent to grab David, Saul himself comes and strips naked and prophesies for a day and a night, and the same saying is again given as the etiology.

The apologist line is that both episodes contributed to the proverb's currency — the saying became proverbial in chapter 10 and got reinforced in chapter 19. Archer and Walter Kaiser run this. It's not implausible on its face, but it ignores the textual signal. Both passages use the etiological formula "therefore it became a proverb" or "wherefore they say," which is Hebrew narrative shorthand for "this is the event that produced the saying." Doing that twice for the same saying is textbook source-doublet behavior.

The critical reading is that 1 Samuel preserves two independent traditions about Saul and ecstatic prophecy, one positive (chapter 10) and one humiliating (chapter 19), and the redactor included both with their separate etiologies intact. McCarter, Hertzberg, and Auld all treat these as parallel traditions rather than sequential events. The two stories serve opposite theological functions — chapter 10 legitimates Saul through prophetic experience, chapter 19 delegitimates him by showing his prophetic frenzy as pathetic and out of control. The Deuteronomist had both traditions in his sources and kept both, even though the etiological formulas can only really work once.

The "both events contributed" defense is functionally an admission that one of the two narrators is wrong about being the origin. Either chapter 10 "originated" the saying and chapter 19 is a later application, or chapter 19 originated it and chapter 10 is anachronistic, or both narrators are independently claiming to be the origin and at least one is wrong. The text won't let you have one neat answer. That is exactly the signature of compiled source material rather than unified composition.

entries.question: When was the last time that Samuel saw Saul?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 15:35 states emphatically that "Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death." 1 Samuel 19:24 then has Saul stripping naked and prophesying before Samuel during the David-pursuit episode. The narrator first closes the door on Samuel/Saul contact, then opens it again four chapters later.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 15:35 is unambiguous. After Samuel hews Agag to pieces and rebukes Saul over the Amalek incident, the chapter closes: "And Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul." That is a categorical end-of-relationship statement. Then in 1 Samuel 19:24, Saul shows up at Naioth in Ramah where Samuel is staying with the prophet band, gets overwhelmed by the spirit, strips, and prophesies in Samuel's presence. The text says explicitly that Saul "prophesied before Samuel" — Samuel is right there.

The apologetic harmonization reads 1 Samuel 15:35 as "Samuel did not visit Saul socially" or "in his official prophetic capacity" — meaning the chance encounter in chapter 19 doesn't violate it because Saul came to Samuel, not the other way around. Archer takes this line, and Tsumura defends a version of it. Hebrew lo' yasaf shemu'el lir'ot et-sha'ul, literally "Samuel did not continue to see Saul," can grammatically support "did not seek out" rather than "did not see at all."

The Hebrew can technically bear that, but the verse explicitly extends the no-seeing "until the day of his death," and the parallel verse in 1 Samuel 28 has the witch of Endor summoning Samuel's ghost specifically because Saul has no living prophet to consult — Samuel will not deal with him. The narrative logic of 1 Samuel as a whole is that Samuel withdrew from Saul permanently after Amalek. Hertzberg, McCarter, and Auld all treat 19:24 as an originally independent tradition spliced into the David-flight narrative, originally unconnected to 1 Samuel 15:35. The redactor put them together without resolving the contradiction. The witch-of-Endor episode in chapter 28 effectively re-confirms 15:35 — Samuel and Saul have not seen each other in life since chapter 15.

There is also a reading where 19:24 is actually a doublet of 10:11-12 with the same proverb-etiology (see entry 229) and so the entire scene is a literary repetition rather than a separate event. If that is right, the "meeting" in 19:24 is a doublet artifact, not a chronological problem. Either way — splicing of independent traditions or doublet of chapter 10 — the parsimonious explanation is compositional, not historical. The apologetic "Samuel didn't initiate the visit" reading is grammatically possible but theologically forced and ignores the rest of the Samuel cycle.

entries.question: When David fled to Nob, what was the priest's name?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech as the priest at Nob who feeds David the showbread. Jesus in Mark 2:25-26 references the same incident and attributes it to "Abiathar the high priest." The Synoptic parallels in Matthew 12 and Luke 6 quietly drop the name.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that has launched a thousand harmonization attempts because it sits in the mouth of Jesus himself. 1 Samuel 21:1 is unambiguous — David came to Nob, the priest was Ahimelech, Ahimelech gave him the showbread. Abiathar was Ahimelech's son (1 Samuel 22:20) and only became high priest after his father was butchered by Doeg at Saul's order. So at the time of the showbread incident, Abiathar was not the high priest. Mark has Jesus saying he was.

The apologetic moves here are extensive. Move one: the Greek epi Abiathar archiereos can be translated "in the passage about Abiathar the high priest" (using epi as a textual reference marker like 12:26's "in the passage about the bush"). This is the favored move of D. A. Carson in his Matthew commentary and is endorsed by Craig Blomberg. Move two: Abiathar was high priest at the time of the writing of the narrative and so Mark uses his more famous title proleptically. Move three (Archer): Ahimelech is Abiathar's father in some texts and his son in others (cf. 2 Samuel 8:17), so there may be two priests named Ahimelech and Abiathar functioning together, and Jesus is right.

The textual data is brutal on these defenses. Matthew 12:3-4 and Luke 6:3-4 both repeat the Mark story and both drop the name Abiathar entirely. The Synoptic-redaction inference is obvious: Matthew and Luke noticed the error and silently fixed it. Bart Ehrman in Jesus, Interrupted explicitly walks through this case, as does Joel Marcus in the Anchor Bible Mark commentary. Marcus rejects the "in the passage about" reading because epi with a genitive proper name in this construction in Mark almost universally means "during the time of" or "in the lifetime of" — Marcus cites Mark 12:26 itself, where epi tou batou ("in the passage about the bush") uses a different construction with a definite article that 2:26 lacks. Move three (two priest pairs) requires assuming the narrative is genealogically chaotic precisely where Jesus speaks, which is unfalsifiable special pleading.

The most parsimonious account: Mark made a mistake, or Mark's source made a mistake, or the historical Jesus made a mistake about an Old Testament detail. Matthew and Luke noticed and silently corrected. The harmonization industry depends on a grammatical reading of epi that the Markan Greek does not naturally support, and it requires both later evangelists to have independently dropped the name without comment, which is itself evidence they saw the problem.

entries.question: Was David alone when asking for the holy bread at Nob?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 21:1 has Ahimelech ask David "why art thou alone, and no man with thee?" — implying David arrived solo. Jesus in the Synoptic Gospels (Matthew 12:3-4, Mark 2:25-26, Luke 6:3-4) explicitly says David's companions ate the showbread with him. The Old Testament source says David came alone; Jesus says he had companions.
entries.commentary:
Reading 1 Samuel 21 in context, the loneliness is the point of the scene. Ahimelech is afraid when David arrives without an entourage — "why art thou alone, and no man with thee?" David lies in response, claiming the king sent him on a secret mission and that he has "appointed his servants to such and such a place." So David is concealing his fugitive status by pretending his men are stationed elsewhere; the men are not present at the showbread transaction. Then David asks for "five loaves of bread" specifically — which all three Synoptics latch onto as evidence that David had companions.

The apologetic harmonization runs like this: David's men were nearby but not at the moment of the bread request, and David collected the bread to bring back to them. Archer, Blomberg, and Carson all take this line. The five-loaves request supports the idea that David was provisioning multiple people. So Jesus's framing — "David and they that were with him" — is technically accurate in context even though the actual scene at Nob has David appearing alone.

The critical reading is more complicated. The companions in 1 Samuel 21 are a fiction David invents to cover his solo flight; the text does not actually confirm they exist. When David next appears in 22:1 he goes to the cave of Adullam alone and his family then "and every one that was in distress" rallies to him there. So the companions whose existence Jesus presupposes either (a) were already with David at Nob (contradicting 21:1's solitude) or (b) joined him afterward at Adullam (in which case Jesus is wrong that they ate the showbread). The five-loaves request can be read as part of David's cover story rather than a real-need-for-companions inventory.

This is a softer contradiction than the Abiathar one because the Synoptic gospel writers had a hand in framing the incident to support their Sabbath-violation argument — Jesus needs the showbread story to feature multiple people eating in violation of priestly law so it parallels his disciples plucking grain. Mark's framing of David "and they that were with him" may be loose with the source text precisely because Mark needs the parallel to hold. Ehrman, Marcus, and Collins all note this redactional pressure on the showbread tradition. The simpler reading is that the Synoptic Jesus is shaping the David story to fit his argument, and the original 1 Samuel narrative has David functionally alone.

entries.question: Was Abiathar the father or the son of Ahimelech?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 22:20, 23:6, and 30:7 consistently identify Abiathar as the son of Ahimelech. 2 Samuel 8:17, 1 Chronicles 18:16, and 1 Chronicles 24:6 reverse the relationship and call Ahimelech the son of Abiathar. The genealogy contradicts itself across the two main historical books.
entries.commentary:
The 1 Samuel data is consistent and detailed: Abiathar escapes the massacre at Nob in 22:20 as "one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub." He shows up with the ephod at 23:6 as "Abiathar the son of Ahimelech." In 30:7 David addresses him as "Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech's son." This is a sustained, multi-attestation identification.

Then 2 Samuel 8:17 lists David's court officials: "Zadok the son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, were the priests." 1 Chronicles 18:16 repeats this — "Abimelech the son of Abiathar" (textual variant). 1 Chronicles 24:6 again has "Ahimelech the son of Abiathar." Three witnesses for the reversed relationship in the Chronicler's tradition and one in 2 Samuel.

The apologetic harmonization is that there were two pairs of Ahimelech/Abiathar — that Abiathar named his son after his father, which was common Israelite practice. So in 1 Samuel we meet Abiathar son of the elder Ahimelech, and in 2 Samuel 8:17 and Chronicles we meet a younger Ahimelech who is Abiathar's son. Archer runs this, as does Keil-Delitzsch in their commentary on Samuel.

The critical-scholarship account is that 2 Samuel 8:17 contains a textual corruption — McCarter, Anderson, and Wellhausen all argue the original read "Abiathar son of Ahimelech, son of Ahitub" and a scribe swapped the names. Wellhausen's emendation has been widely accepted; the Lucianic recension of the LXX may preserve the corrected form. This is one of the rare cases where the apologetic two-pairs solution and the critical scribal-error solution converge on the same outcome — the relationship really is Abiathar-son-of-Ahimelech — but they disagree on whether the MT of 2 Samuel/Chronicles is reliable. The apologetic move keeps the MT inerrant and posits a second priest pair the text never explicitly identifies. The critical move admits a scribal error preserved in the MT.

Either way, the surface text contradicts itself. The harmonization either invents undocumented family duplicates or concedes textual corruption. Take your pick — but you can't have both an inerrant MT and a consistent genealogy.

entries.question: Did Saul inquire of the Lord?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 28:6 says explicitly that Saul inquired of the Lord and the Lord refused to answer. 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 says Saul died because he "inquired not of the Lord." The two texts disagree about whether Saul's failure was that he tried and got no answer, or that he never tried.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 28:6 is unambiguous: "And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets." Saul tried every legitimate channel of revelation. The text frames the witch-of-Endor consultation as a desperate last resort after Yahweh ghosted him. 1 Chronicles 10:13-14 retells Saul's death and offers this theological summary: "So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD ... and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to inquire of it; and inquired not of the LORD: therefore he slew him." The Chronicler's verdict is that Saul did not inquire of Yahweh at all.

The standard apologetic harmonization is that the Chronicler means Saul did not inquire properly or did not inquire with a faithful heart. Archer, Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Chronicles commentary, and Andrew Hill in NIVAC Chronicles all run versions of this. The Hebrew verb darash means both "to inquire" and "to seek with proper devotion," and so the Chronicler is supposedly emphasizing the quality of Saul's seeking rather than its existence.

The critical reading rejects that as semantic overreading. The Chronicler is doing what the Chronicler routinely does — rewriting the Deuteronomistic History to underline a theological point. The Deuteronomist in 1 Samuel 28 tells a complicated story: Saul did the right thing first (inquired of Yahweh, got nothing), then did the wrong thing (consulted a necromancer). The Chronicler simplifies and moralizes: Saul died because he was a covenant-breaker who went to a medium instead of Yahweh. The Chronicler erases the inconvenient detail that Saul actually tried Yahweh first, because that detail complicates the theology.

Sara Japhet, Ralph Klein, and Gary Knoppers all treat this as a paradigmatic case of the Chronicler's theological revisionism. Japhet specifically notes that the Chronicler's account of Saul's death (in his single chapter on Saul before pivoting to David) is calibrated to make Saul a pure foil for David, and any mitigating circumstances in Samuel are dropped. The harmonization that wants both 1 Samuel and 1 Chronicles to be precisely accurate has to twist darash to mean two different things in two texts. The simpler reading is the Chronicler is doing redaction-with-an-agenda, and it shows.

entries.question: Was Jesus the first to rise from the dead?
entries.summary: Acts 26:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:20 call Jesus the firstfruits of the resurrection and the first to rise from the dead. But the witch of Endor in 1 Samuel 28:11-14 raises Samuel from the dead centuries earlier, and the Hebrew Bible has Elijah and Elisha raising others (1 Kings 17, 2 Kings 4, 2 Kings 13), as does Jesus himself in the Gospels (Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, the widow of Nain's son). Jesus is not chronologically first.
entries.commentary:
Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:20 calls Christ "the firstfruits of them that slept," and Acts 26:23 has Paul before Festus claiming Christ would be "the first that should rise from the dead." These are theological claims. The Hebrew Bible has the witch of Endor explicitly raising Samuel — "an old man cometh up; and he is covered with a mantle. And Saul perceived that it was Samuel" — and Samuel speaks at length to Saul before predicting Saul's death. Elijah resuscitates the widow's son in 1 Kings 17, Elisha resuscitates the Shunammite's son in 2 Kings 4, and 2 Kings 13:21 has a corpse revive on contact with Elisha's bones. In the Gospels, Jesus himself raises Lazarus, Jairus's daughter, and the Nain widow's son — all chronologically before Jesus's own resurrection.

The standard apologetic distinction is between resuscitation (returning to mortal life, eventually dying again) and resurrection (immortal eschatological body, never dying again). Paul's claim is that Jesus is the first to undergo the latter. N. T. Wright in The Resurrection of the Son of God makes this argument at length — Samuel, Lazarus, et al. were resuscitated to mortal life and died again, while Jesus rose with a glorified body that does not die. Acts 26:23's "first that should rise from the dead" is read as eschatological-resurrection-specific.

This distinction works for Paul but has a problem for the Samuel case. Samuel in 1 Samuel 28 is not resuscitated to mortal life — he's brought up from Sheol in a spectral form, speaks, and presumably returns. If the apologist wants "resuscitation vs. resurrection" to do the work, then Samuel's appearance is neither, and the verse can be discarded as not really being a "rising from the dead." But that just means the SAB has picked a weak example. The Lazarus and Jairus's-daughter examples are tighter — Jesus does explicitly raise people from the dead before his own resurrection, and those resurrections happen in the same Gospel narrative.

The Wright distinction is theologically coherent but it is post-hoc to Paul's text. Paul does not say "Christ is the first to rise with a glorified body" — he says Christ is the firstfruits. The apologist read requires reading "firstfruits" as a technical eschatological-body marker rather than a chronological one. That is plausible but it is exegesis-by-need. The simpler reading is that Paul is making a theological claim that doesn't bother to harmonize with the pre-Christian Jewish revival traditions. The Hebrew Bible writers and the synoptic gospel writers did not share Paul's framework, and the texts disagree on whose resurrection counts as the first.

entries.question: Did Saul and Samuel kill all the Amalekites?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 15:7-8 says Saul utterly destroyed all the Amalekites with the edge of the sword. The same chapter lets Agag's mother survive (15:33), David is still slaughtering Amalekites years later in 1 Samuel 27:8 and 30:1-17 (with 400 escaping), and an Amalekite kills Saul in 2 Samuel 1:8-10. The text contradicts its own "utterly destroyed all" claim multiple times within a few chapters.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 15 is the herem chapter — total annihilation, every man, woman, infant, suckling, and livestock except what Saul illicitly spared. Verses 7-8: "Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, that is over against Egypt. And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword." Then in the very same chapter, verse 33: Samuel tells Agag "as the sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women." Agag's mother is alive, which means the "all the people" of verse 8 was not actually all the people.

It gets worse. 1 Samuel 27:8-9 has David raiding the Amalekites ("David and his men went up, and invaded the Geshurites, and the Gezrites, and the Amalekites: for those nations were of old the inhabitants of the land"). 1 Samuel 30:1 has Amalekites still numerous enough to sack Ziklag, and David's revenge slaughter in 30:17 explicitly lets 400 escape. Then 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite present at Saul's death — the very people Saul allegedly exterminated produce his executioner. And in Esther, centuries later, an Agagite is grand vizier of Persia (see entry 221).

The apologetic position is that "utterly destroyed all" is ancient Near Eastern war-rhetoric hyperbole, not a literal claim. Paul Copan in Is God a Moral Monster?, Nicholas Wolterstorff, and Richard Hess all argue this from the comparative ANE evidence — Egyptian, Assyrian, and Moabite (Mesha Stele) royal inscriptions routinely claim total annihilation that was demonstrably not literal. The point of the rhetoric is decisive victory, not census-accurate body count. Lawson Stone defended a version of this for the Joshua conquest narratives.

The hyperbole reading is genuinely well-supported by comparative epigraphy. The Mesha Stele's claim that Omri "utterly destroyed" Israel is a useful parallel — Israel demonstrably persisted. So the rhetorical-hyperbole defense has real evidentiary backing. But it cuts both ways. If you concede 1 Samuel 15:8 is hyperbolic, you are conceding the text reports things that did not literally happen — and the same standard then has to apply to Joshua, Judges, and elsewhere. The herem texts cannot be both literal divine commands and convention-bound rhetoric. The apologist who wants Yahweh's command to be a real moral act AND the report to be hyperbolic ANE convention has a tension to resolve. Most critical scholars (McCarter, Hertzberg, Klein, Niditch) just call it what it is: the chapter is a stylized theological narrative in which the literal claims do not have to harmonize with later chapters because the genre does not demand it.

entries.question: How did Saul die?
entries.summary: 1 Samuel 31:4-6 and 1 Chronicles 10:4 say Saul committed suicide by falling on his sword. 2 Samuel 1:8-10 has an Amalekite claim he killed Saul at Saul's request. 2 Samuel 21:12 says the Philistines killed Saul. 1 Chronicles 10:14 says Yahweh personally killed him. Four different causes of death across four different texts.
entries.commentary:
1 Samuel 31:4 has Saul, gravely wounded, ask his armor-bearer to finish him off. The armor-bearer refuses out of fear, so Saul falls on his own sword. The armor-bearer then falls on his own sword too. 1 Chronicles 10:4 repeats this account essentially verbatim. So far, suicide.

2 Samuel 1:8-10 then has an Amalekite show up to David after the battle, claim he found Saul leaning on his spear, and that Saul personally asked the Amalekite to kill him because Saul was sure to die anyway. The Amalekite says he killed Saul and took the crown to David. 2 Samuel 21:12 says "the Philistines had slain Saul." 1 Chronicles 10:14 wraps up the death narrative with "the LORD ... slew him."

The traditional apologetic harmonization works through each claim. Suicide is the literal physical cause (1 Samuel 31, 1 Chronicles 10:4). The Amalekite is lying in 2 Samuel 1 to curry favor with David — David executes him anyway, but his story is fabricated. The Philistines "slew Saul" in 2 Samuel 21:12 in the sense that they put him in the situation that led to suicide; the Hebrew makah can mean "struck" in a broader sense. And Yahweh "slew him" in 1 Chronicles 10:14 theologically — every death is ultimately God's doing in the Deuteronomistic-Chronistic worldview. Archer, Youngblood, and Walter Kaiser all run versions of this stacked harmonization.

The Amalekite-was-lying answer is the strongest of the apologetic moves and is genuinely defensible — David's reaction (executing the Amalekite as if for regicide) only makes sense if the Amalekite's story is taken at face value within the narrative even if the narrator implicitly doubts it. McCarter and Anderson both note this is possible. The other harmonizations work but only by allowing the verb "to kill" to do progressively more metaphorical work across the texts. The Philistines did not literally kill Saul; they were the proximate threat. Yahweh did not literally kill Saul; he is the theological cause behind the historical event. Stack enough of those reinterpretations and you can harmonize any death account — but only by treating the texts as if they were all answering different questions.

The critical reading is that these are independent traditions about Saul's death, each making a different theological point. The Deuteronomist in 1 Samuel 31 wants Saul as the tragic suicide. The court history in 2 Samuel 1 wants the David-clears-his-conscience-of-Saul's-blood story, which requires a non-David killer. The Chronicler wants Saul's death as divine judgment for covenant breach. Each tradition foregrounds a different cause. They don't synthesize into one historical account — they reflect different theological agendas applied to a shared event. The apologetic synthesis works on paper but it requires four different definitions of "killed" to function.

entries.question: Did Saul's family die with him?
entries.summary: 1 Chronicles 10:6 says "Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." 2 Samuel 2:1-7 then has Ishbosheth — Saul's son — made king of Israel after Saul's death. 2 Samuel 21 has David later handing over seven of Saul's descendants to be hanged. The "all his house died together" claim is contradicted by surviving family members appearing throughout 2 Samuel.
entries.commentary:
1 Chronicles 10:6 is sweeping: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and all his house died together." The parallel in 1 Samuel 31:6 is narrower — "so Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together." The Chronicler globalizes "all his men" into "all his house."

The rest of Samuel demolishes the Chronicler's globalization. Ishbosheth, Saul's son, is made king over Israel by Abner in 2 Samuel 2:8-11. He reigns two years. Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, survives and ends up at David's table (2 Samuel 9). Rizpah, Saul's concubine, is alive in 2 Samuel 3 and 2 Samuel 21. And 2 Samuel 21:1-14 has David hand over seven of Saul's male descendants — Rizpah's two sons Armoni and Mephibosheth, plus the five sons of Saul's daughter Merab — to be hanged by the Gibeonites to end a famine. That is at minimum nine living members of Saul's house after the events of 1 Samuel 31.

The apologetic harmonization is the standard Chronicler-summary defense: the Chronicler is making a theological point about the end of Saul's dynastic legitimacy, not a literal census claim. Archer and Hill both argue "all his house" means "the rest of his fighting men with him at Gilboa" rather than every blood relative. Eugene Merrill in his Kregel Chronicles commentary takes a similar line, reading "house" as the military household rather than the family.

This reading has Hebrew lexical support — bayit ("house") can mean dynasty, family, or fighting unit depending on context. But the Chronicler's redactional move is doing more work than the apologist concedes. The Chronicler's account of Saul is a single chapter, structured to terminate Saul completely so David's kingship has no genealogical competition. Japhet, Klein, and Knoppers all argue the Chronicler deliberately compresses and exaggerates the end of Saul's house to underscore the theological discontinuity. The Chronicler knows about Ishbosheth — he just doesn't include him because Ishbosheth complicates the narrative. The contradiction is real at the surface level, but it is a deliberate Chronistic literary decision, not a factual error in the modern sense. Either way, the bare-text claim of 1 Chronicles 10:6 — that Saul's whole house died at Gilboa — is contradicted by the narrative of 2 Samuel that the Chronicler is supposedly summarizing.

entries.question: Who was David's second son?
entries.summary: 2 Samuel 3:3 names David's second son born in Hebron as Chileab, son of Abigail. 1 Chronicles 3:1 names David's second son born in Hebron as Daniel, son of Abigail. Same mother, same birth-order slot, different name.
entries.commentary:
Both texts give the same list of David's first six sons born in Hebron in the same order, with the same mothers — except the second name. 2 Samuel 3:3 has "his second, Chileab, of Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite." 1 Chronicles 3:1 has "the second Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess." Position matches, mother matches, name doesn't.

The apologetic harmonization is that this person had two names — Chileab and Daniel — and each text preferred one. Archer takes this line. Keil-Delitzsch and Youngblood agree. Multi-naming is well-attested in the Hebrew Bible (Jacob/Israel, Solomon/Jedidiah), and it's not unreasonable on the surface.

The textual-critical reading is messier. Some manuscripts of 2 Samuel and Chronicles show further variation: certain LXX manuscripts of 2 Samuel 3:3 read Daluyah or Daluiah, and the Lucianic recension preserves still other forms. McCarter argues the original name was probably Daniel ("God is my judge"), Chileab is a Hebrew variant or corruption, and the Daluyah readings reflect intermediate confusion. Anderson in WBC and Auld in OTL note the same textual messiness. Sara Japhet on Chronicles also flags the variant tradition.

The double-name hypothesis is possible but undocumented — neither text actually says "also called." The textual-variation hypothesis is documented — we have manuscript witnesses with different readings, suggesting scribal evolution of the name across transmission. Either way, the contradiction is at the textual surface. The apologist can save the inerrancy of both names only by positing an unmentioned dual identity; the critical scholar treats it as ordinary textual variation. This is a relatively minor contradiction — names are easy to corrupt in transmission — but it is real on the canonical surface, and the harmonization is post-hoc.
